summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style article on the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), an 8-bit home console developed by Nintendo that launched as the Famicom in Japan in 1983 and was later released in North America, Europe and Australia. It covers Nintendo's market influence over third-party developers, the failed Atari deal, the marketing response to the 1983 video game crash, the console's bundles, the AV Famicom redesign, the Famicom's development, and efforts to block unlicensed games.
one_line: Nintendo's 8-bit home console, released as the Famicom in Japan in 1983, covering its launch, bundles, redesigns, development and anti-piracy measures.
key_facts: The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) is an 8-bit home video game console developed and manufactured by Nintendo.
The NES was initially released in Japan as the Family Computer (Famicom) on July 15, 1983.
The console was released in North America during 1985, in Europe during 1986, and in Australia in 1987.
In South Korea the console was known as the Hyundai Comboy and was distributed by SK Hynix, then known as Hyundai Electronics.
The NES was succeeded by the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.
Nintendo had planned to release the Famicom under Atari's name as the Nintendo Advanced Video Gaming System, but Atari's CEO Ray Kassar was fired the next month and the deal fell through.
The video game market crash of 1983 was partly due to confusion and misrepresentation in video game marketing, such as bombastic packaging artwork that exaggerated graphics.
The Deluxe Set retailed at US$199.99 (equivalent to $475 in 2016) and included R.O.B., a light gun called the NES Zapper, two controllers, and two Game Paks: Gyromite and Duck Hunt.
The Basic Set retailed at US$89.99 with no game, and US$99.99 when bundled with Super Mario Bros.
The Action Set retailed in 1988 for US$149.99 and came with the Control Deck, two game controllers, an NES Zapper, and a dual Game Pak with Super Mario Bros. and Duck Hunt.
The Challenge Set of 1992 included the console, two controllers, and a Super Mario Bros. 3 Game Pak for US$89.99.
The AV Famicom, released in December 1993, used composite video output instead of RF only, and dropped hardwired controllers in favor of detachable controller ports.
Masayuki Uemura designed the Famicom, and president Hiroshi Yamauchi rejected a planned advanced 16-bit computer-like system in favor of a cheaper cartridge-based console.
Early Famicom games were written on a system running on an NEC PC-8001 computer, with LEDs on a grid and a digitizer used to design graphics.
Companies that refused to pay licensing fees or were rejected by Nintendo tried to circumvent the NES authentication system, mostly by using voltage spikes to temporarily disable the 10NES chip.
Nintendo of America threatened retailers who sold unlicensed games with losing their supply of licensed titles.
